Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up swiftly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

Industry observers note that this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

According to recent reports, pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Industry observers note that even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

It has been revealed that the useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

Recent findings suggest that with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

Industry observers note that this distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Sources indicate that rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Recent findings suggest that calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

It has been revealed that pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

According to recent reports, the first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives patch the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

It has been revealed that cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

In a recent development, the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

It has been revealed that the complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

Recent findings suggest that the script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

In a recent development, sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

Industry observers note that you can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

According to recent reports, both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

Industry observers note that at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

In a recent development, the gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

According to recent reports, if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

It has been revealed that multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

Recent findings suggest that with a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that during a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle.
  • Recent findings suggest that in Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint.
  • Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that during a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it.

Recent findings suggest that in Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters.

Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1.

According to recent reports, models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions.

Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself.

The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own.

The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate.

“At Bagelcode, we run our own LLM inference service on AWS to help teams across the tech giant, including our game teams, use AI to improve how they work. In our beta tests, the Global Inference Gateway in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod routed requests across two AWS Regions through a single endpoint and kept serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave our small platform team cross-Region failover without having to build or maintain our own routing layer.”.

— Jinhyung Park, VP (AI Platform), Bagelcode.

Setting up the gateway takes two decisions: which clusters to open up for routing, and which of them to group behind one gateway.

Recent findings suggest that A cluster is reachable only after you publish it. When you publish a cluster, the controller creates a Network Load Balancer in front of the cluster’s Inference Gateway, publishes a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service on it, and uploads the listener’s certificate to your TLS bucket. These resources live in your account. If you list a cluster in a gateway before you publish it, the call fails with a message that tells you what to fix.

According to recent reports, figure 1 highlights the path of each request: (1) your client signs the request with SigV4 and sends it to the gateway’s regional endpoint. (2) The gateway authenticates the caller and picks the best cluster. (3) AWS PrivateLink carries the request to that cluster, in the same Region or another, and (4) the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod, as it does today.

Figure 1: The Global Inference Gateway receives each request at one regional endpoint and forwards it over AWS PrivateLink to the best HyperPod cluster, where the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod. Each cluster publishes its load back to the gateway.

You decide which clusters to publish, which to group behind a gateway, and how to weight routing. AWS operates the rest:.

On each cluster, a service-managed metrics publisher with its own IAM role sends the cluster’s load to the gateway.

For each request, the gateway scores every healthy cluster on four signals and sends the request to the highest-scoring cluster. Each cluster’s metrics publisher supplies the load signals.

Recent findings suggest that you control how much each signal counts with routing weights. Each weight is a value from 0.0 to 1.0, and a weight of 0 turns that signal off. If you set weights, you set all four, and they must add up to 1.0. If you omit them, the defaults in the following table apply.

The defaults favor clusters close to the gateway’s Region, while still moving traffic toward clusters with available capacity and away from clusters that are failing. If resilience matters more than proximity for your workload, raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity. For example, the following routing block weights recent errors at 0.7:.

You pass the weights in the Routing parameter of CreateGlobalInferenceGateway, and you can change them later with UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway.

Recent findings suggest that your path depends on what you run today. If you serve from a single cluster, stay on that cluster’s Inference Gateway endpoint. Move to the Global Inference Gateway when you add a second cluster.

To set up the Global Inference Gateway, you prepare each cluster, create an execution role, and call CreateGlobalInferenceGateway. You then send OpenAI-compatible requests, signed with SigV4, to the gateway endpoint. For step-by-step instructions, including the IAM roles and policies, see the AWS documentation.

In a recent development, every request to the gateway is signed with SigV4 and authorized with IAM. Callers need permission to invoke the gateway, and streaming has its own action:.

Attach this policy to each IAM identity that sends requests. To allow every gateway in the account, use global-inference-gateway/* as the resource.

Industry observers note that the execution role follows least privilege. It can describe only the clusters you list, reach only their Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) API, and read only the routing certificates under the gig/ prefix of your TLS bucket, tagged as created by HyperPod Inference.

According to recent reports, identity tokens. If your clusters check JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), pass the token with --customer-identity-token (the X-Amzn-SageMaker-Customer-Identity-Token header), with no Bearer prefix. The token travels inside the SigV4 signature, so an unsigned token is rejected with 403 and a repeated token with 400. Turn on JWT checks on every cluster that serves a model, or on none of them, so a request doesn’t succeed on one cluster and fail on another.

Requests reach your clusters only through AWS PrivateLink, as shown in Figure 1. The gateway does not log or store prompts or completions.

Here are steps to configure the gateway.

Industry observers note that prepare the latest cluster and create the execution role’s EKS access entry on it, as described in the documentation. Also add the new cluster to the Resource lists of the execution role’s permissions policy. Then call AddInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region, even if the new cluster is in another Region:.

The gateway validates the cluster and starts routing to it once it is healthy. The endpoint, other clusters, and clients aren’t affected.

Call RemoveInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region:.

In a recent development, the gateway stops sending latest requests to the cluster, lets in-flight requests finish, and removes the private endpoint. A gateway always keeps at least one cluster. To withdraw the cluster fully, set globalRouting.enabled: false in its InferenceGatewayConfig and reapply it.

Call DeleteGlobalInferenceGateway:.

Sources indicate that the gateway endpoint stops serving, and per-cluster endpoints keep serving. After the gateway is deleted, withdraw each cluster with globalRouting.enabled: false, then delete the execution role and the IAM permissions you added for global routing.

For any troubleshooting assistance, please see the Troubleshooting Guide.

In this post, we introduced the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: one SageMaker-managed endpoint across your HyperPod clusters, in one Region or several. The gateway picks the cluster based on KV cache headroom, queue depth, Region proximity, and error rate, and moves traffic off a failed cluster with no client changes.

Sources indicate that the Global Inference Gateway is available in 13 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

To get started, see the AWS documentation.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (213 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.33563v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) leveraging large language models (LLMs) aims to harness their strengths in knowledge integration, logical reasoning, and text generation for efficiently producing innovative, verifiable scientific hypotheses. However, existing approaches face three critical limitations: (i) insufficient fine-grained knowledge representation, as unstructured context impairs LLM comprehension and reasoning; (ii) lack of knowledge evolution traceability, constraining the generation of innovative cross-domain conjectures; (iii) absence of human-inspired and role-specialized multi-agent collaboration, failing to leverage the efficient innovation mechanisms arising from cognitive diversity and division of labor among expert roles to complete the full ASHG-evaluation loop. To address these limitations, we propose the Fine-grained Inspiration Graph-empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration framework (FIG-MAC) including: (i) Fine-grained Inspiration Graph module (FIG), to obtain fine-grained structured knowledge representations, where nodes represent academic semantic units and edges encode heuristic relationships among them; (ii) ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module, which follows the FIG ontology to construct structured reasoning paths and uses vector search to enrich them with semantic evidence, to obtain the traceable scientific conjecture paths; (iii) role-specialized Multi-Agent framework, inspired by real scientific teamwork, enabling a closed-loop process of scientific conjecture generation, screening, and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that FIG-MAC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty.

arXiv:2611.33555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.

Breaking: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • It has been revealed that building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

It has been revealed that building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps owners entirely in control of their digital lives.

Recent findings suggest that botPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

Sources indicate that we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

It has been revealed that finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

Sources indicate that botPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Industry observers note that table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

It has been revealed that botPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Recent findings suggest that table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

According to recent reports, complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

Recent findings suggest that botPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

Recent findings suggest that it does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

Industry observers note that botPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

In a recent development, botPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#11409. Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes.
  • We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure.
  • Industry observers note that in this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its consumers in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do.

We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance.

Industry observers note that in this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them.

We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section.

Figure 1: The Slurm cluster configuration stack.

Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration, administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database. HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it, minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests.

Automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them.

Recent findings suggest that the five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. As researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, and an exporter ships a fix. For this layer, lifecycle scripts have been the main mechanism so far, and they have drawbacks when the software keeps changing. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet. A mistake reveals only when the script runs on a node, and nothing reports what’s installed, so nodes drift apart over time.

We wanted the software to be declared in one place, checked when you submit it, kept consistent across nodes, and visible afterward. In November 2026, we released cluster extensions, which are software packages managed by AWS that you install, configure, revision, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console, starting with observability and user management, including directory integration, as the first software extensions. Compared with scripts, extensions have these advantages:.

Use cluster extensions when HyperPod offers a managed software capability. Use custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software or initialization that the available extensions don’t cover. HyperPod supports two cluster managed extensions today:.

The following diagram indicates how an extension reaches your nodes.

It has been revealed that figure 2: HyperPod can install, edit, or remove an extension. HyperPod records the desired configuration, a node agent applies the extension package on every node, including latest and replaced ones, and health probes report status and health issues back.

Sources indicate that you can use cluster extensions from the SageMaker AI console or through an API. On the console, the Extensions tab on a cluster’s details page lists each extension with its status, version, and ARN, and it’s where you install a newly introduced one. Each extension adds controls of its own, such as the metric store and an open dashboard in Grafana button for observability, and the number of customers and groups and a Manage users button for user management. You can also manage every extension through APIs, from the AWS CLI or an SDK, to script installs, keep settings in version control, repeat a setup across clusters, or check status and health from your own tooling. The following table lists the six cluster extension APIs, from installing an extension to listing the versions you can upgrade to, along with console view for extensions.

Sources indicate that figure 3: Left, the six cluster extension APIs and what each one does. Right, the console view to add and remove extensions.

The following diagram demonstrates what happens after you call one of these APIs.

According to recent reports, figure 4: You declare an extension’s version and settings through the API. HyperPod validates and records them, applies them to every node for its role, and reports status and health.

Recent findings suggest that when you create or enhancement an extension, HyperPod validates your settings against the version’s schema during the API call, so a misspelled setting is rejected immediately. It then records the version and settings as the desired state and applies them, with each node installing only what its role needs, such as GPU exporters on GPU nodes only. Latest and replacement nodes get the same state a few minutes after they start, and every node reports whether the extension applied and whether it’s healthy.

According to recent reports, updates send only the settings that you want to change, and HyperPod merges them into the stored settings. Problems that show up only on a node, such as a port or user ID that something else already uses, appear in the Health field of DescribeClusterExtension, grouped by cause with a code, a message, and a count of affected nodes. HyperPod retries internal failures on its own, and for anything else you fix the cause and call UpdateClusterExtension with no changes to retry the affected nodes.

An extension’s status is Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem, and Degraded when some nodes failed or report a problem. Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own sagemaker-user-management while a monitoring team owns sagemaker-observability. Each health issue names the component, describes the effect on your cluster, gives the next step, and counts the affected nodes, so you can see where to look without signing in to each node, as the following figure shows.

Figure 5: An extension’s status, and an example health concern for a node exporter that isn’t running.

A useful way to decide is to ask who owns the software and how often it changes. Some of the software on a cluster is specific to your organization, such as security agents, license servers, and the storage layout your data pipeline expects. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs are the right tools for it, because only your team knows what it needs. The rest is software that almost every cluster needs, like GPU and job metrics and user accounts with consistent IDs and access rules. That software must match on every node and keeps changing, so cluster extensions are the better fit, because you declare it once, HyperPod validates it, and each extension reports whether it’s healthy.

In a recent development, the two approaches can coexist, but each component should have one owner. Don’t manage the same exporter, user, or service through both a lifecycle script and an extension, because competing configurations can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Cluster extensions work with every lifecycle configuration option.

If you already run these capabilities from scripts, you can move to extensions one capability at a time, and scripts and extensions can run side by side while you do. For each capability, the migration takes four steps:.

Sources indicate that if anything is left behind, the install names the conflict, such as a port that’s already in use, and DescribeClusterExtension reveals it under Health. With user management, you keep the same usernames and user IDs. The following figure shows four steps.

Figure 6: Moving an existing cluster from lifecycle scripts to extensions, one capability at a time.

You need a HyperPod Slurm cluster on or after the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later with continuous provisioning enabled. An extension runs software as root on every node, so treat CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension, and DeleteClusterExtension as administrator permissions. We suggest that you do not grant them to the cluster’s execution role, because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use its credentials. That role does need access to the destinations that the extensions use, which means Amazon CloudWatch or aps:RemoteWrite for observability and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the Active Directory secrets that user management reads. If those secrets are encrypted with a customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key, the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key. User management also needs a shared file system, such as Amazon FSx for Lustre, for home directories.

For procedures, IAM policies, and configuration references, see Cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

To see how cluster extensions are used in practice, consider a platform team that manages a shared Slurm cluster for several research groups. The team needs a reviewable cluster definition, GPU and job metrics, corporate directory access, local accounts for a partner lab, and separate ownership of observability and user management. The following examples show how the team configures these capabilities and responds to routine changes and failures.

It has been revealed that the administrator declares the whole cluster, including node roles, partitions, FSx mounts, minimum capacity, deep health checks, and the external accounting database, in a single CreateCluster request. For a complete example request, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI.

Sources indicate that the request has no lifecycle configuration, topology file, or Slurm configuration file. Each SlurmConfig gives its instance group a role, and the GPU group joins the train partition. AMI-based configuration sets up the nodes, and the security team’s compliance agent is already in the custom AMI. The GPU group asks for 8 nodes and requires 6, so jobs can start as soon as 6 are ready while HyperPod provisions the rest and health checks each GPU node as it arrives. HyperPod selects tree topology for the P5 nodes on its own, and accounting writes to an Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database that the team owns. The administrator can still SSH into the controller node to inspect or tune Slurm directly.

It has been revealed that leadership wants GPU and job metrics, so the administrator installs the observability extension. In the SageMaker AI console, on the cluster’s Extensions tab, the administrator chooses the observability extension, picks the metric categories and their levels and the collection interval, and selects one of two metric stores: Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. The following screenshot shows the install form with one store selected. The other option is available in the same field.

Figure 7: Installing the observability extension from the console, with configurable metric levels and a choice of metric store.

According to recent reports, the same installation through the API takes one create-cluster-extension call. The following example uses Amazon CloudWatch as the metric store. To send metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus instead, you set the Prometheus destination in the same configuration.

The administrator installs the extension with one create-cluster-extension call:.

The call returns the extension’s ARN, which the administrator uses in later calls:.

Whichever way it’s installed, each node runs only the components relevant to its role, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller. Schema errors are rejected before rollout, while node-specific conflicts appear in extension health.

After the install, the extension appears on the cluster’s Extensions tab with its version, status, and ARN. The screenshot highlights the tab for a cluster that has both the observability and user management extensions installed, and both are Active.

Figure 8: The Extensions tab for a cluster with both the observability and user management extensions installed.

Whichever metric store you choose, you can add an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace to the installation, so the team doesn’t need to build dashboards from scratch. After signing in to Grafana, they find two pre-created dashboards, Clusters and Jobs, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 9: The Clusters and Jobs dashboards that come with the observability extension in Amazon Managed Grafana.

In a recent development, the Clusters dashboard gives a single view of your HyperPod Slurm clusters, built on the metrics that the extension collects and sends to your chosen metric store. At the top, it summarizes cluster health: instance count and health, GPU and GPU memory totals, vCPUs, memory, and Amazon FSx for Lustre capacity. It also demonstrates the state of Slurm itself, including node states (idle, allocated, mixed, down, and draining), job queues, failed or preempted jobs, and scheduler activity. From there, you can filter by cluster, node, or GPU to drill into EFA networking, GPU performance and errors, and host-level CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics, as shown in the following screenshots. That lets you go from “is my cluster healthy?” to the root cause of an glitch without leaving the dashboard.

Figure 10: The Clusters dashboard, from cluster-wide health and Slurm state down to per-node GPU, EFA, and host metrics.

The Jobs dashboard moves from cluster-level health down to individual Slurm jobs. It ties each job’s resource to use back to the job itself, using metrics from the Slurm job exporter in either metric store. You can filter by cluster, job ID, job name, partition, user, or account, and see CPU, memory, GPU utilization, GPU memory, and disk I/O for each job, plus accelerator and NCCL metrics. That makes it easier to spot underused GPUs, stuck jobs, or communication bottlenecks in distributed training, as in the following screenshot.

Figure 11: The Jobs dashboard, showing resource use for individual Slurm jobs.

Later, a research team that is tuning multi-node training asks for more detail, so the administrator sends only the settings to change:.

According to recent reports, hyperPod merges these settings into the stored configuration and applies them to every node, restarting only the components whose settings changed. When the investigation is over, setting both to null returns them to their defaults, and at no point are nodes replaced or scripts rerun.

In a recent development, one morning the extension highlights as Degraded. A upcoming instance group has an execution role that lacks aps:RemoteWrite, and describe-cluster-extension shows the effect:.

Once the administrator adds the permission, the nodes report healthy and the extension returns to Active, with nothing to reinstall.

According to recent reports, the user management extension manages the Linux owners and groups on every node, and who can sign in and use sudo on each node type. You declare who should exist and what they can do, and HyperPod applies it to every node, including nodes added later or replaced, so no one connects to nodes or runs scripts to add or remove a user. Users come from local accounts that you list in the configuration, from Active Directory over LDAPS, or from both, and each group names the node types (controller, login, or compute) where its members can sign in over SSH and where they get passwordless sudo.

Recent findings suggest that for the platform team, security wants corporate identities, with sudo reserved for administrators, and a partner lab that isn’t in the directory needs accounts of its own. The administrator declares both sources in one configuration, with group rules that say which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on:.

In a recent development, access is explicit, so after the extension is installed only the groups that grant SSH access, along with the default ubuntu user, can sign in. Directory people keep their identities and group membership in Active Directory, while the partner lab’s users get the same IDs, home directories, and the default Slurm root account.

Industry observers note that the same configuration can be managed from the console. Choosing Manage users on the user management extension opens the cluster’s Users tab, where the administrator can add, edit, and remove groups and users, and set which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 12: Managing groups and customers for the user management extension on the console.

When AWS publishes a new version of an extension, the administrator lists the versions that can be installed and upgrades in place without AMI updates:.

According to recent reports, hyperPod checks the stored settings against the latest version’s schema and rejects the request, changing nothing, if they aren’t valid for it. Otherwise, the new version rolls out to every node, and nodes that join later get it too. Upgrades only go forward, so the administrator picks a maintenance window. Any new settings or capabilities that come with the version can then be turned on with an update like the earlier one.

Before the end-of-quarter run, the administrator starts an on-demand deep health check on the GPU group and then adds nodes with batch-add-cluster-nodes. The request returns as soon as HyperPod accepts it, so the administrator follows it as a cluster operation:.

As capacity arrives, each node is health checked, joins Slurm, takes its place in the topology, and gets both extensions with the same version and settings as every other node. If a GPU fails during the run, the replacement is configured and picks up the extensions the same way.

At the end of the quarter, security asks who has sudo on the controller, and the administrator answers from the API without signing in to a node:.

It has been revealed that the answer is cluster-admins and ClusterAdmin@example.com, and the directory group’s membership is audited in the directory. Because each extension has its own ARN, the platform team’s role can enhancement only sagemaker-user-management and the monitoring team’s role only sagemaker-observability, while security has read-only access to both. None of these permissions belongs on the cluster’s execution role. When an extension is Active, ActiveCount equals TotalCount, and Health is empty, every node runs exactly that configuration.

Recent findings suggest that cluster extensions, including the observability and user management extensions, have been available since November 2026 in all the regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is supported, and the other improvements in this post were unveiled earlier in 2026, with each announcement listing its Regions. There’s no additional charge for cluster extensions. You pay for the AWS resources that you use with them, such as Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and AWS Secrets Manager.

Figure 13: The two extensions that have been available since November 2026.

In a recent development, A cluster is easier to run when more of it is declared, validated, converged, and observable. This year’s improvements brought that to a HyperPod Slurm cluster’s definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health, and cluster extensions, available since November 2026, bring it to the software on the nodes, the layer that changes most often. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs stay focused on what’s specific to your organization, and the controller node stays yours.

To create a cluster as described in this post, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI. To get started with cluster extensions, see Cluster Extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Share your feedback in the comments or through your AWS account team.

Sources indicate that this feature has contributions across several teams. Some of the people involved in developing this include Hengyu Lou, Aman Pratap Singh, Karthick Ravi, Shubh Nisar, Nitish Sai Kommasai, Uday Singamala, Min Badar, Devanshi Desai, Yahya Hassan, Connie Chen, Kashish Tayal, Oleg Talalov, Takuma Yoshitami, Kiran Penta, Dhawal Parkar, Pradeep Cruz.

#11406. Learning to Reason in Real-Time

Learning to Reason in Real-Time

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (221 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they at the moment do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.

#11404. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2596 w)
